title: The Boasting Traveller
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Man once went abroad on his travels, and when he came home he had wonderful tales to tell of the things he had done in foreign countries. Among other things, he said he had taken part in a jumping-match at Rhodes, and had done a wonderful jump which no one could beat. "Just go to Rhodes and ask them," he said; "every one will tell you it's true." But one of those who were listening said, "If you can jump as well as all that, we needn't go to Rhodes to prove it. Let's just imagine this is Rhodes for a minute: and now--jump!"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Man have to tell when he comes home?
options: News of a war he had witnessed abroad
Complaints about the hardships of travel
Wonderful tales of what he did in foreign countries
A list of goods he had traded overseas

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Man claim to have done at Rhodes?
options: A wonderful jump which no one could beat
Won a wrestling match against a champion
Built a bridge admired by the whole city
Sailed a ship through a great storm

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Man say people in Rhodes will tell you?
options: That they don't remember him
That the match never happened
That someone else jumped farther
That it's true

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the listener suggest instead of going to Rhodes?
options: Writing to someone in Rhodes to confirm the story
Imagining the spot they are standing in is Rhodes, and jumping right there
Waiting for someone from Rhodes to visit and confirm it
Finding an old newspaper report of the match

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what single word does the listener use to challenge the Man directly?
options: "Prove it!"
"Liar!"
"Jump!"
"Really?"

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the listener propose imagining the spot as Rhodes?
options: To test the Man's claim immediately instead of relying on distant witnesses
To make the game more entertaining for the crowd
To help the Man remember exactly how he jumped
To give the Man a fair second chance at Rhodes itself

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Man's claim rely so heavily on people far away in Rhodes?
options: He genuinely believes someone will travel there to confirm it
He wants his listeners to visit Rhodes for their own enjoyment
He forgot the exact details of the jump himself
Distant witnesses cannot be easily checked, making the boast harder to disprove

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "abroad" mean in "went abroad on his travels"?
options: To a nearby village
To a foreign country
To a mountain retreat
To a family gathering

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean that no one "could beat" the Man's jump?
options: No one could see it happen
No one could describe it accurately
No one could match or surpass it
No one could attempt it safely

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable, given its closing line?
options: Actions can be tested here and now, while boasts about the past cannot
Travelling to foreign countries always leads to exaggeration
Jumping contests are an unreliable measure of skill
It is rude to challenge someone's stories in public

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where does the Man claim his famous jump took place?
options: Athens
Sparta
Corinth
Rhodes

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what kind of tales does the Man bring back from his travels?
options: Frightening ones
Wonderful ones
Sad ones
Short and simple ones

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the listener say about needing to travel to Rhodes?
options: That they must go there at once
That Rhodes is too far to ever visit
That they needn't go there to prove it
That Rhodes no longer holds such contests

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what is the listener really asking the Man to do with the challenge to jump?
options: Demonstrate the skill immediately rather than merely describe it
Travel back to Rhodes to repeat the jump properly
Apologize for exaggerating his travels
Teach the listener how to jump as well as he claims to

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the story end right at the moment of the challenge rather than showing the jump itself?
options: The Man is given time to travel back to Rhodes first
The listener changes his mind before the jump happens
The passage simply ran out of space to describe more
The unanswered challenge itself is enough to expose the boast as empty

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "deeds" mean in the closing line "Deeds, not words"?
options: Legal documents of ownership
Actual actions performed
Spoken promises to others
Stories told for entertainment

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A man successfully repeats his famous jump for a cheering crowd
A man is praised for his honesty about his travels
A man who boasts about a distant feat is challenged to prove it on the spot
A group of listeners travel to Rhodes to confirm the story
